questions.q: A random variable X has E[X] = 2 and E[X²] = 8. What is Var(X)?
Why is linearity of expectation, E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y], so useful for portfolio math?
options: It only works when returns are normally distributed
It holds regardless of how X and Y depend on each other, so expected portfolio return is just the weighted sum of expected asset returns
It requires X and Y to be independent
It only applies to discrete random variables
questions.explain: Linearity of expectation is unconditionally true for any random variables and any constants — no independence or distributional assumption is required.

questions.q: An equity return series has skewness of -0.8. What does this indicate?
options: Returns have a longer, heavier left tail than right tail — large negative moves are more extreme than large positive ones
questions.explain: Negative skewness means the left tail is longer or fatter than the right tail — it describes the asymmetry of the distribution's shape, not the sign of the mean.

questions.q: A normal distribution has kurtosis equal to 3. What does an excess kurtosis of +2 on a return series tell you?
options: The returns have negative average value
The distribution has fatter tails than a normal distribution, so extreme moves occur more often than a normal model predicts
The returns are independent of each other
questions.explain: Excess kurtosis is kurtosis minus 3. A positive excess kurtosis means heavier tails than the normal distribution — more frequent extreme outcomes than a normal model would suggest.

questions.q: X and Y are independent random variables with Var(X) = 4 and Var(Y) = 9. What is Var(X + Y)?
questions.explain: For independent random variables, Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) = 4 + 9 = 13 (the covariance cross-term vanishes under independence).
